title: Lennard-Jones clusters on the face-centred cubic lattice
statement: Place N atoms on distinct sites of the face-centred cubic lattice: integer points (x, y, z) with x + y + z even, nearest neighbours at squared distance 2. Every pair of atoms interacts by the Lennard-Jones potential with the nearest-neighbour distance at the potential's minimum, so a pair at squared distance q contributes 64/q^6 - 16/q^3 in units of the well depth (exactly -1 for nearest neighbours), with the usual cutoff at 2.5 sigma: only pairs with q <= 8 (the first four shells) count. Energies are exact rational numbers. Which N-atom clusters have the lowest energy? The headline cell is N = 100: find a cluster of 100 atoms with energy below -789723697/1492992 = -528.953737 (ours).
submission: Text file: 100 lines 'x y z', distinct integer points with x + y + z even.
score: the energy, an exact rational number (smaller is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: simulated annealing over clusters started from the sites nearest a random centre, moving one atom at a time to a site next to the cluster, many restarts in 60 seconds (tools/src/ljfcc.c)

context: Clusters of rare-gas atoms bound by the Lennard-Jones potential are the standard test of global optimisation: the best known minima are tabulated up to 1,610 atoms (the Cambridge Cluster Database), and their structure changes with size, icosahedral for most small clusters, decahedral or face-centred cubic for some, and face-centred cubic in the bulk crystal. Lattice searches build candidates on icosahedral, decahedral or fcc lattices before relaxing them (Northby 1987; Shao, Cheng and Cai 2004). Keeping the atoms on fcc sites, with the bond length at the potential minimum and no relaxation, gives a purely combinatorial problem with exact rational energies: the most stable N-atom piece of an fcc crystal under the Lennard-Jones interaction with the standard cutoff at 2.5 sigma (four shells of neighbours). Nearest-neighbour bonds dominate (the 13-atom cuboctahedron has 36 of them), but the second, third and fourth shells reward compact shapes beyond counting bonds, and clusters with the same number of bonds are separated by those pairs. Exact minima are not known to us for any N beyond the smallest; the table gives our best clusters.
references: J. A. Northby, Structure and binding of Lennard-Jones clusters: 13 <= N <= 147, J. Chem. Phys. 87 (1987) 6166-6177
D. J. Wales, J. P. K. Doye, Global optimization by basin-hopping and the lowest energy structures of Lennard-Jones clusters containing up to 110 atoms, J. Phys. Chem. A 101 (1997) 5111-5116
X. Shao, L. Cheng, W. Cai, A dynamic lattice searching method for fast optimization of Lennard-Jones clusters, J. Comput. Chem. 25 (2004) 1693-1698
The Cambridge Cluster Database (D. J. Wales et al.), https://www-wales.ch.cam.ac.uk/CCD.html

novelty.verdict: new question: Lennard-Jones minima are tabulated for relaxed clusters, and lattices serve only to generate candidates; no one posed the minima restricted to fcc sites (2.5 sigma cutoff, exact energies) as a question of their own.
closest: The Cambridge Cluster Database and basin-hopping minima (Wales and Doye 1997): relaxed clusters in continuous space; here the atoms stay on lattice sites and energies are exact.

Lattice searching methods (Northby 1987: icosahedral lattice; Shao, Cheng and Cai 2004 and later: fcc and decahedral lattices): use lattice clusters as starting points and relax them; the unrelaxed fcc minima are not reported as a problem of their own.
novelty.benchmark: no cluster or lattice-gas family in the benchmark

first_values.note: Energies from the exact checker (checkers/orig_chem.py, cutoff q <= 8); clusters from tools/src/ljfcc.c, 60 s for each N. No lower bound beyond the trivial one is known to us.

baseline.text: -789723697/1492992 = -528.953736524 (435 nearest-neighbour pairs), held by Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: the cluster in `refs/lj-fcc.txt`.
